```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Idea A's demand evidence is stronger. It has three independent, first-person accounts of production incidents caused by upstream API changes, from dev.to, r/SaaS and r/Backend. Idea B's strongest demand evidence comes from Trunk, a flaky-test vendor describing its own tooling, plus one Reddit comment.",
    "Idea A's price hypothesis rests on published self-serve prices from direct competitors: apidrift.co at $29/mo and Nalvis at $14/mo. That shows small teams are being offered self-serve pricing at roughly the target level, which fits a 90-day first sale. Idea B borrows its price from an enterprise add-on via a third-party aggregator, and its closest competitor (Develocity) hides pricing behind contact-sales. Idea B's own brief says this suggests the category leans toward negotiated enterprise deals.",
    "Idea A's product delivers value on day one: watch for a change, diff it, open a PR. Idea B has a cold-start problem its own brief admits. New installs have no test history to learn from, and buyers may need months of track record before letting the tool gate merges. Both work against getting paid within 90 days.",
    "Both ideas face crowded fields and false-positive or false-negative trust risk. Idea A's risk is partly contained because a human reviews every PR before merge. Idea B's worst case is silently skipping a real failure, which its sources say destroys the trust the tool is meant to restore.",
    "Idea B carries extra friction for a solo operator. Its brief says a DPA and security review are likely if code is sent to an LLM. Its core technique also doesn't strictly need an LLM, which weakens differentiation against free OSS tools."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "Idea B's lead demand quote and its '20.2M CI jobs' statistic both come from a HackerNoon article by Trunk, a vendor selling flaky-test tooling. That is promotional content, not independent buyer demand. Separately, B's two unsourced claims (six-week MVP, free founder-time acquisition) count as missing.",
  "weakest_evidence_in_winner": "Idea A's CAC benchmark ($248 median, 9.4-month payback) comes from a page that contained a prompt-injection attempt. The brief itself rates it directional only, so it should be treated as unreliable.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-to-low confidence. Both briefs show crowded markets with free alternatives, and neither has direct willingness-to-pay evidence such as a customer saying they would pay. Idea A wins mainly on more independent demand signals and proven self-serve price points. It still faces the open question of why SMBs would pay $20-50/mo when three competitors offer this free."
}
```
